column3: The hill above Hong Kong Island with the classic view of skyscrapers, Victoria Harbour and Kowloon. It is especially magical at dusk, when the lights come on.
A steep cable railway that has carried passengers up to Victoria Peak since 1888, with a ride that feels almost vertical.
The business heart of Hong Kong, with glass towers, old markets, trams and the bank buildings that line the harbor.
A small, sloping lane in Central packed with bars and restaurants, a hub of nightlife.
A temple for Man, the god of literature, and Mo, the god of war, with large incense coils hanging from the ceiling.
A busy shopping district with department stores, street food and bright signs, and the noon gun that is fired each day.
A seaside village on the south side of Hong Kong Island with a market, a waterfront promenade and old temples.
One of the most popular beaches on Hong Kong Island, with a curve of golden sand, apartments and a Kwun Yam shrine.
A marine theme park built on a hillside, with rides, aquariums, pandas and a cable car above the sea.
A chain of escalators and walkways about 800 meters long that carries people up the steep hill from Central to the Mid-Levels.
A sweet bun with a crusty, cookie-like top that looks like a pineapple, but has no pineapple. It is best eaten warm, with a slab of butter.
A strong black tea mixed with evaporated milk and strained through a cloth bag, silky smooth. It is Hong Kong's favorite drink.
A bubble-shaped waffle with a crisp shell and a soft center, cooked in a special mold, sold hot from street stalls.
Crisp-skinned roast goose with juicy meat, a Hong Kong favorite that is often served with plum sauce and rice.
Thin, springy egg noodles in a clear broth with shrimp wontons, a Hong Kong classic with a long tradition.
A tart with a flaky or crumbly crust and a smooth, golden custard. It is a staple of bakeries and teahouses.
The Hong Kong-style café that serves toast, noodles, rice dishes and milk tea. It is a fast, noisy and friendly part of the city's life.
Roast meats such as char siu, roast pork and goose hang in shop windows, and are served over rice.
Cantonese opera, with its glittering costumes and sung stories, is still staged in Hong Kong, in large temporary bamboo theaters at festivals.
Hong Kong cinema is famous for kung fu films, crime thrillers and romances, with stars such as Bruce Lee, Jackie Chan and Chow Yun-fat.
On Cheung Chau, the Bun Festival has towers of sweet buns, parades and lion dances, to ask the gods for peace.
At the Dragon Boat Festival, teams of paddlers race long, painted boats to the beat of a drum.
A promenade on the Kowloon waterfront with handprints and statues of film stars, facing the skyline of Hong Kong Island.
A bustling harbor district of Kowloon with shops, hotels, museums, and the Clock Tower beside the water.
A night market with stalls for clothes, trinkets, fortune tellers and street food, at its liveliest in the evening.
One of the most densely populated areas in the world, with neon signs, crowded streets and endless shops.
A market street where stalls sell clothes, bags and accessories at low prices, and bargaining is expected.
A garden market where men hang cages with songbirds and trade them. The air is full of birdsong.
A Buddhist nunnery in Tang-dynasty style, built of wood without nails, set in a quiet garden of lotus ponds.
A classical Chinese garden with ponds, rocks, wooden pavilions and bonsai, next to the nunnery. It offers calm in the city.
A busy Taoist temple where people shake fortune sticks, and ask for health and luck.
A park on the site of the old Kowloon Walled City, once an enclave of dense, tall buildings that was torn down in the 1990s.
Fish balls on a stick or in a bowl, covered in a spicy curry sauce, a classic Hong Kong street snack.
Cart noodles are a bowl of noodles to which you add toppings, such as beef brisket, radish and fish balls, in a rich soup.
Dim sum are bite-sized dishes served in bamboo steamers with tea. Dumplings, buns and rolls are shared by the family around a table.
A sweet dessert soup, from red bean to mango with sago, served warm or cold after a meal.
A steamed open dumpling filled with pork and shrimp, topped with an orange dot, found at every dim sum meal.
A plate of fried rice with egg, char siu or shrimp, stir-fried until each grain is separate and fragrant.
Feng shui is the art of arranging buildings, doors and water according to the flow of qi, and it shapes many of Hong Kong's skyscrapers.
A giant bronze Buddha, 34 meters high, sits on a hill on Lantau Island, with 268 steps leading up to it. Monks at the nearby monastery serve vegetarian meals.
A long cable car ride over the sea and mountains of Lantau to Ngong Ping, with views of the airport and the South China Sea.
A fishing village of stilt houses over the water, where you can take a boat to look for pink dolphins and try shrimp paste.
A seaside town known for its seafood restaurants, country parks, beaches and islands with volcanic rock columns.
A theme park on Lantau Island, with rides, shows and characters, built in a smaller style than other Disney parks.
A city in the New Territories with a river, a racecourse, a big shopping mall and a large heritage museum.
A hillside monastery with thousands of small golden Buddha statues along its steps, and a hall with a preserved monk.
A small, car-free island with beaches, seafood, and a big bun festival, an easy ferry ride from Central.
A car-free island with hiking trails, seafood restaurants and quiet villages, where life is calm and slow.
Tai O is known for its shrimp paste, a salty, strong-smelling paste used in cooking and in sauces.
A big basin that is layered with meats, seafood, tofu and vegetables, eaten from the top down, a village feast tradition.
Fresh fish and shellfish are picked from tanks and cooked right away at the waterfront restaurants of Sai Kung.
Sweet buns stamped with a red character for peace, piled into towers at the festival and eaten for luck.
Walled villages built by clans for protection, with thick walls and gates, some with their own temples and ancestral halls.
The Tanka, or boat people, lived their whole lives on boats in the harbor and have their own songs and customs.
